input:
In this example we consider the conduction of heat through a flat
firebrick wall, with the object of determining the heat flux by
means of Fourier's law, which relates the flux to the properties
of the wall and to the temperature difference maintained across it.
The wall in question is flat, it has a thickness of 150 mm, and its
thermal conductivity $k$ is 1.1 W m-1 K-1. Firebrick is a
refractory material, which is to say that it is capable of
withstanding furnace temperatures that few structural materials
could tolerate, and its conductivity is low, so that a wall built
from it serves the double purpose of containing the furnace and
limiting the heat that escapes through it. The temperature
difference $\Delta T$ across the wall is 382 K, and the thickness,
converted into metres, is $\Delta x$ = 0.15 m.

For the case of steady one-dimensional conduction, the flux is
computed by the relation

$$q = k \frac{\Delta T}{\Delta x}$$

in which $q$ denotes the heat flux, $k$ the thermal conductivity,
$\Delta T$ the temperature difference and $\Delta x$ the wall
thickness. The description steady indicates that the temperatures
do not change with time, while one-dimensional indicates that the
temperature varies only through the thickness, uniformly over the
face of the wall, so that a single gradient is sufficient to
describe the whole wall. Substituting the values, $q$ = 1.1 x 382 /
0.15 = 2801 W m-2.

Two points of caution complete the example. The calculation
excludes the film resistances at the two faces of the wall, and
since a surface film adds its own resistance in series with the
wall, the flux through the real construction, with the films
included, would be lower than 2801 W m-2. The value obtained,
2801 W m-2, is thus the flux through the wall alone, and it should
be read as an upper figure for the assembly of which the wall forms
a part.
target:
Heat passes through a flat firebrick wall by conduction, and
Fourier's law gives the flux from the wall properties and the
temperature difference across the wall. The heat flux $q$ is
2801 W m-2.

The wall is flat, its thickness is 150 mm, and its thermal
conductivity $k$ is 1.1 W m-1 K-1. Firebrick is a refractory
material: it withstands furnace temperatures that few structural
materials tolerate, and its conductivity is low, so a wall of it
both contains the furnace and limits the heat lost through it. The
temperature difference $\Delta T$ across the wall is 382 K. The
thickness, expressed in metres, is $\Delta x$ = 0.15 m.

For steady one-dimensional conduction, the flux is computed by

$$q = k \frac{\Delta T}{\Delta x}$$

where $q$ denotes the heat flux, $k$ the thermal conductivity,
$\Delta T$ the temperature difference and $\Delta x$ the wall
thickness. Steady means that the temperatures do not change with
time; one-dimensional means that the temperature varies only
through the thickness, uniformly over the face of the wall, so that
a single gradient describes the whole wall. Heat flows through the
wall from the hot face towards the cold face, in the direction of
falling temperature. The flux is a rate per unit area: a larger
wall passes more heat in total at the same flux, because the
gradient through it and the material of it are unchanged.
Substitution gives $q$ = 1.1 x 382 / 0.15 = 2801 W m-2.

The calculation excludes the film resistances at the two faces of
the wall. A surface film adds its own resistance in series with the
wall, so the flux through the real construction, films included, is
lower than 2801 W m-2. The stated value is therefore the flux
through the wall alone, and it stands as an upper figure for the
assembly of which the wall forms a part.
